title: DevOps and Delivery
description: How software is built, packaged, shipped and run reliably: CI/CD, containers, Kubernetes and infrastructure as code.
audience: A capable adult who can write and read code and use a terminal, and who wants to understand how changes reach production and stay running. No prior operations experience.
outcomes: You'll be able to measure delivery performance and explain why small batches reduce risk.
You'll be able to design a pipeline and choose a rollout strategy for a given risk.
You'll be able to explain what a container is, build an efficient image and read a run command.
You'll be able to describe Kubernetes as a reconciliation system and compute rolling-update and autoscaling numbers.
You'll be able to read declarative infrastructure code, an error budget and the main supply-chain risks.

sources.title: DORA research programme: software delivery performance metrics
Docker documentation: Get started, Build, Dockerfile reference
sources.licence: Docs repository Apache-2.0 per its repo; confirm before adapting

sources.title: Open Container Initiative specifications (image and runtime)
The Site Reliability Workbook (Google), chapters on SLOs and alerting

modules.title: Delivering change safely
modules.summary: Why small, frequent, automated change is safer than rare, large release, and how pipelines and rollout strategies make it so.

modules.title: Containers
modules.summary: What a container is, how images are built in layers, and how containers are run and wired together.

modules.title: Kubernetes
modules.summary: Declared desired state, the objects that run and expose workloads, and how they scale and take configuration.

modules.title: Infrastructure as code and operation
modules.summary: Describing infrastructure in files, reconciling it from Git, observing it, and keeping the supply chain trustworthy.

lessons.title: Why shipping is the hard part
lessons.objective: Measure a team's delivery performance with the four DORA metrics and explain why smaller batches lower risk.

concepts.title: Lead time for changes
concepts.summary: The time from a commit being made to that commit running in production.

concepts.title: Change failure rate
concepts.summary: The share of deployments to production that cause a failure needing remediation, such as a rollback or hotfix.

concepts.title: Batch size
concepts.summary: The amount of change shipped together; larger batches make failures harder to locate and to undo.

misconceptions: Frequent deployment is reckless: in the data speed and stability rise together, because small changes are easy to understand and to reverse.
DevOps is a job title or a toolchain; it is a way of working in which the team that builds a change also owns running it.
Lead time means the time to write the code; it begins at commit and ends in production.
sequence: Start from a Friday release that takes forty changes at once and ask which one broke checkout.
Define the four measures: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service.
Show that the measures pair a speed with a stability, so one cannot be gamed alone.
Argue from batch size: with one change in a release the cause of a failure is known; with forty it must be searched for.
Name the cultural point: the people who write the change share responsibility for how it runs.
examples: 12 deployments in 4 weeks is 3 a week; 6 failing of 48 deployments is a 12.5 per cent change failure rate.
A commit at Monday 09:00 reaching production on Wednesday 15:00 has a lead time of 54 hours.

figures.shows: Four rows (frequency, lead time, failure rate, restore time), each with a team's number and a speed or stability tag.
figures.learnerAction: Fill a team's figures and watch which pairs move together.

figures.shows: Two timelines: one release of 40 changes with a failure, one of 40 single-change releases with a failure marked on one.
figures.learnerAction: Tap the failing release and mark the candidate causes remaining.

questionPlan.sample: A team makes 12 production deployments in 4 weeks. How many deployments a week is that?
6 of a team's 48 deployments needed a rollback or hotfix. What is the change failure rate as a percentage?
A commit is made Monday 09:00 and reaches production Wednesday 15:00. What is the lead time in hours?

historyNotes: The DORA programme began as the State of DevOps reports (first published 2014) and was later led by DORA at Google Cloud; the 2024 reports renamed time to restore service as failed deployment recovery time. Check the current wording before quoting.

lessons.title: Version control for continuous change
lessons.objective: Choose a branching approach that keeps integration frequent, and say what a merge conflict is a symptom of.

concepts.title: Commit graph
concepts.summary: Git stores history as a graph of commits, each identified by a hash of its content and its parents.

concepts.title: Trunk-based development
concepts.summary: Developers integrate small changes into one shared branch at least daily, keeping other branches short-lived.

concepts.title: Merge conflict
concepts.summary: Two changes edit the same lines, so the tool cannot decide which to keep.

misconceptions: A branch is a copy of the files; it is a movable pointer to a commit.
Long-lived feature branches are safer because they isolate risk; they defer the integration problem and make it larger.
Merge conflicts mean someone did something wrong; they are the cost of delaying integration.
sequence: Draw four commits and two branch pointers to show that branching copies nothing.
Contrast a branch alive for three weeks with one alive for a day: how many other commits land meanwhile.
Introduce trunk-based development and feature flags as the way to merge unfinished work safely.
Cover pull requests and review as a gate on the shared branch, with small diffs.
Link back to batch size from the previous lesson.
examples: A branch that lives 15 working days while 6 developers each merge 2 commits a day has fallen behind by 6 x 2 x 15 = 180 commits.
A pointer moved with git switch -c fix creates no new commit.

figures.shows: A commit graph with main and two branches, labelled with hashes.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the branch pointer to a different commit and see which commits become reachable.

figures.shows: Two weeks of merges by day for long-lived versus short-lived branches.
figures.learnerAction: Slide the branch lifetime and read the commits behind.

questionPlan.sample: A feature branch lives 15 working days. 6 other developers each merge 2 commits a day to main. How many commits has main gained by the time the branch merges?
What does creating a branch in Git do?
questionPlan.answer: It creates a new movable pointer to a commit
choices: It copies every file to a new folder
It creates a new movable pointer to a commit
It uploads the code to a server

questionPlan.sample: Which practice best lets unfinished work be merged to the shared branch daily?
questionPlan.answer: Hide it behind a feature flag
choices: Keep the branch private until it is finished
Hide it behind a feature flag

lessons.title: Continuous integration and the pipeline
lessons.objective: Design a pipeline whose stages give the fastest useful feedback and compute its wall-clock time.

concepts.title: Continuous integration
concepts.summary: Every change is built and tested automatically, on a clean machine, as soon as it is pushed.

concepts.title: Pipeline
concepts.summary: An ordered set of stages, some running in parallel, that a change passes through before release.

concepts.title: Build artifact
concepts.summary: A versioned, immutable output of the build that every later stage and environment reuses unchanged.

misconceptions: The pipeline should run the slowest tests first; cheap, fast checks should come first so failure is reported early.
Rebuilding the code for each environment is fine; it breaks the guarantee that what was tested is what ships.
Green CI means the software is correct; it means only that the checks that exist passed.
sequence: Show a failed push at minute 1 versus minute 28 and what each costs the author's focus.
Separate the commit stage (build, unit tests, lint) from slower stages (integration, deploy).
Introduce parallelism and sharding as ways to cut wall-clock time without cutting checks.
Build once, promote the same artifact through environments.
Mention a pipeline defined as code in the repository, with a current example such as GitHub Actions or GitLab CI.
examples: Sequential: lint 2, build 5, unit 8, integration 12, deploy to staging 3 is 30 minutes. Build first, then lint, unit and integration in parallel, then deploy: 5 + 12 + 3 = 20 minutes.
A 32-minute test suite split into 4 equal shards takes 8 minutes if the shards are balanced.

figures.shows: A pipeline as boxes with durations, with parallel lanes.
figures.learnerAction: Drag stages between sequential and parallel lanes; the total time updates.

figures.shows: Six stages to put in order of feedback speed.
figures.learnerAction: Arrange them.

questionPlan.sample: Build takes 5 minutes. Then lint (2), unit tests (8) and integration tests (12) run in parallel. Then deploy to staging takes 3. How many minutes does the pipeline take?
A 32-minute test suite is split into 4 equal shards that run in parallel. How many minutes does it take, ignoring set-up time?
Which check belongs first in a pipeline?
questionPlan.answer: The cheapest check that catches the most common failures
choices: The cheapest check that catches the most common failures

lessons.title: Releasing without fear
lessons.objective: Select a rollout strategy for a given risk and explain how feature flags separate deploying from releasing.

concepts.title: Deploy versus release
concepts.summary: Deploying puts code on servers; releasing exposes it to users, and a flag can separate the two.

concepts.title: Canary release
concepts.summary: A new version receives a small share of traffic while its error rate is compared with the old version.

concepts.title: Blue-green deployment
concepts.summary: Two full environments exist; traffic is switched from the live one to the idle one, and back to roll back.

misconceptions: Rolling back is always possible; a migration that drops a column cannot be reversed by redeploying old code.
Blue-green is free; it needs capacity for two environments at the switch.
A canary tests the code; it tests the code under real traffic, only if someone watches the right metric.
sequence: Describe the three: rolling replaces instances in batches, blue-green switches whole environments, canary shifts a percentage.
Work the traffic arithmetic for a canary.
Show why database changes need an expand-then-contract sequence to stay reversible.
Introduce feature flags and their cost: stale flags are debt.
Tie to change failure rate and restore time.
examples: 5 per cent of 2,000 requests a second is 100 requests a second to the canary; if it returns errors on 2 per cent of them that is 2 errors a second.
A rolling update of 10 instances, 2 at a time, takes 5 batches.

figures.shows: Three small diagrams of traffic between old and new versions, one per strategy.
figures.learnerAction: Switch views and move a traffic slider on the canary.

figures.shows: Error rate of old and new version over 30 minutes of a canary.
figures.learnerAction: Choose the minute at which to abort.

questionPlan.sample: A service receives 2,000 requests a second. A canary gets 5 per cent. How many requests a second reach the canary?
10 instances are replaced 2 at a time. How many batches does the rolling update need?
Which strategy needs capacity for two full production environments?

lessons.title: What a container is
lessons.objective: Explain a container as an isolated process on a shared kernel and distinguish an image from a container.

concepts.title: Container
concepts.summary: An ordinary process started with its own view of processes, network and files, and with limits on resources.

concepts.title: Image
concepts.summary: A read-only, layered filesystem and metadata from which containers are started.

concepts.title: Namespaces and cgroups
concepts.summary: Linux features that limit what a process can see (namespaces) and what it can use (cgroups).

misconceptions: A container is a lightweight virtual machine; it shares the host kernel, which is why it starts in milliseconds and why a kernel flaw affects all of them.
An image is a running thing; it is a stored template, and many containers can start from one image.
Deleting a container deletes its image; the image remains.
sequence: Start from the problem: it works on my machine, because the libraries differ.
Show a process list on the host that includes the container's process.
Introduce namespaces for what is visible and cgroups for how much may be used.
Contrast with a virtual machine, which runs its own kernel.
Define image versus container, and a registry as the place images are stored.
examples: One image started three times gives three containers, each with its own writable layer.
A container limited to 512 MiB that tries to use 600 MiB is killed by the kernel for exceeding its memory limit.

figures.shows: Layered stack for a VM (hardware, hypervisor, guest OS, app) beside a container (hardware, host OS, runtime, app).
figures.learnerAction: Toggle views; tap a layer to see what it isolates.

figures.shows: One image box with three container boxes each holding a thin writable layer.
figures.learnerAction: Start and stop containers.

questionPlan.sample: Which part of the system do all containers on a host share?
You run one image three times. How many containers exist?
Which Linux feature limits how much memory a container may use?

lessons.title: Building images well
lessons.objective: Order a Dockerfile to use the layer cache, shrink the image with a multi-stage build and avoid baking secrets in.

concepts.title: Layer cache
concepts.summary: A build step is reused if its instruction and everything before it are unchanged.

concepts.title: Multi-stage build
concepts.summary: A build uses one stage with compilers to produce files, and copies only those files into a small final stage.

concepts.title: Secrets in layers
concepts.summary: Anything written in any layer stays in the image history, even if a later step deletes it.

misconceptions: Deleting a file in a later RUN removes it from the image; the earlier layer still holds it.
COPY . . first is simplest and so best; it invalidates the cache on every edit, including dependencies.
Latest is a version; the tag moves, so builds differ over time.
sequence: Show a Dockerfile as a list of layers, each cached by its inputs.
Reorder so dependency files are copied and installed before the source.
Introduce multi-stage builds and the effect on size and attack surface.
Explain tags versus digests, and pinning base images.
Show why a secret copied then deleted is still recoverable.
examples: Changing only src/app.js with COPY package.json, RUN npm ci, COPY src reuses the npm ci layer; reversing the order reruns it.
Build stage 1,200 MB, final stage 180 MB: the shipped image is 180 MB, a saving of 1,020 MB.

figures.shows: Dockerfile lines beside stacked layers coloured cached or rebuilt.
figures.learnerAction: Edit a file and see which layers turn from cached to rebuilt.

figures.shows: Step through the Dockerfile as the builder reads it.
figures.learnerAction: Step.

questionPlan.sample: Dockerfile: FROM node:22 / COPY package.json . / RUN npm ci / COPY src ./src / CMD ["node","src/app.js"]. After editing only src/app.js, how many of the five instructions are rebuilt rather than cached?
A build stage image is 1,200 MB and the final stage copied from it is 180 MB. How many MB smaller is the shipped image than the build stage?
Which Dockerfile keyword begins a stage that can be copied from later, as in FROM golang AS build?

lessons.title: Running and connecting containers
lessons.objective: Read a run command and compose file to say what is published, what persists and which containers can reach each other.

concepts.title: Published port
concepts.summary: A mapping from a host port to a container port, written host:container.

concepts.title: Volume
concepts.summary: Storage managed outside the container's writable layer, which survives the container.

concepts.title: User-defined network
concepts.summary: A virtual network on which containers reach each other by service name.

misconceptions: Data written inside a container is saved; it disappears with the container unless it is on a volume.
-p 8080:80 means container port 8080; the host port comes first.
Containers should be treated as pets that are logged into and repaired; they should be disposable, replaced rather than fixed.
sequence: Run a web server container and publish a port.
Show the writable layer and what is lost when the container is removed.
Add a volume and prove the data survives.
Connect an app and database by service name on one network.
Introduce environment variables for configuration, as in the twelve-factor approach.
examples: docker run -p 8080:80 nginx makes the server answer on host port 8080, while inside the container it listens on 80.
A database writing to /var/lib/db with no volume loses all rows when the container is removed.

figures.shows: Host and container boxes with port arrows and a volume cylinder.
figures.learnerAction: Change the -p mapping and see which URL reaches the app.

figures.shows: A small compose file beside the resulting services and networks.
figures.learnerAction: Remove a volume line and see which data becomes transient.

questionPlan.sample: docker run -p 8080:80 nginx. On which host port can you reach the server?
A database container is removed and recreated with no volume. What happens to its rows?
choices: They are kept in the image
They are kept in the network

questionPlan.sample: What is the name of Docker storage that survives container removal?

lessons.title: Desired state and the control loop
lessons.objective: Explain how Kubernetes keeps a declared state true through reconciliation, and name the control plane and node components.

concepts.title: Desired state
concepts.summary: The object you submit describes what should exist; controllers act until observed state matches it.

concepts.title: Pod
concepts.summary: The smallest deployable unit: one or more containers sharing a network namespace and storage.

concepts.title: Control plane
concepts.summary: The API server, etcd, scheduler and controller manager, which store and act on cluster state.

misconceptions: Kubernetes runs your containers directly; it asks the kubelet on each node to run them, via a container runtime.
A pod is a container; a pod may hold several tightly coupled containers.
A pod that dies is restarted in place; a controller creates a replacement pod, which is a new object with a new IP.
sequence: Contrast imperative commands with a declared manifest.
Walk through the loop: observe, compare, act, repeat.
Name the control plane parts and what each stores or decides.
Name node parts: kubelet, container runtime, kube-proxy.
Trace kubectl apply from request to a running pod.
examples: Desired 3 replicas with 2 running: the controller creates 1; with 4 running it deletes 1.
A pod spec with two containers shares one IP address and can reach each other on localhost.

figures.shows: Cluster diagram: control plane box (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager) and two nodes (kubelet, runtime, pods).
figures.learnerAction: Tap a component to see which request it handles; step through an apply.

figures.shows: Steps from kubectl apply to a running pod.
figures.learnerAction: Put them in order.

questionPlan.sample: A Deployment declares 5 replicas and 3 pods are running. How many pods will the controller create?
Which control plane component stores all cluster state?
Which component on each node ensures the pod's containers are running?

lessons.title: Deployments, labels and Services
lessons.objective: Use labels and selectors to connect Services to pods, and compute the pod counts of a rolling update.

concepts.title: Deployment
concepts.summary: An object that manages ReplicaSets so a set of identical pods can be updated gradually.

concepts.title: Label selector
concepts.summary: A query on labels; Services and ReplicaSets use it to find their pods.

concepts.title: Service
concepts.summary: A stable virtual address and name that load-balances to the ready pods matching a selector.

misconceptions: Pod IPs are stable addresses to use; they change when pods are replaced, which is the reason Services exist.
A Service sends traffic to every pod with matching labels, whether ready or not; only ready pods receive it.
maxSurge and maxUnavailable are counts only; each can be a percentage.
sequence: Show pods churning and breaking direct IP use.
Introduce a Service with a selector, and readiness.
Show a Deployment owning a ReplicaSet, and a new ReplicaSet created on image change.
Explain the rolling update parameters and rounding.
Compare Service types briefly: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer.
examples: 10 replicas, maxSurge 25 per cent rounds up to 3, maxUnavailable 25 per cent rounds down to 2: at most 13 pods exist and at least 8 are available.
3 replicas with maxSurge 1 and maxUnavailable 0: at most 4 pods, at least 3 ready.

figures.shows: Pods as coloured boxes with labels; a Service arrow reaching those matching.
figures.learnerAction: Edit a pod's label and watch the Service endpoints change.

figures.shows: Old and new ReplicaSet pod counts at each step of a rolling update.
figures.learnerAction: Change surge and unavailable values.

questionPlan.sample: A Deployment has 10 replicas, maxSurge 25% and maxUnavailable 25%. What is the greatest number of pods that may exist during the update? (Surge rounds up.)
Same Deployment. What is the fewest pods that must be available? (Unavailable rounds down.)
A Service has selector app=web. Which pods receive traffic?

lessons.title: Configuration, resources and scaling
lessons.objective: Separate configuration from images, set requests and limits sensibly, and compute what the autoscaler will do.

concepts.title: ConfigMap and Secret
concepts.summary: Objects that supply configuration to pods; a Secret is base64-encoded by default, not encrypted.

concepts.title: Requests and limits
concepts.summary: A request is what the scheduler reserves; a limit is the most a container may use.

concepts.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
concepts.summary: Adjusts replica count with desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas x currentMetric / targetMetric).

misconceptions: A Secret is encrypted; by default it is only base64 encoded, so access control and encryption at rest must be configured.
Setting a CPU limit equal to the request is always right; limits throttle CPU and kill on memory, so they need measurement.
More replicas always help; the autoscaler cannot add capacity beyond node supply or a database bottleneck.
sequence: Show config injected as environment variables and files.
Decode a base64 Secret to show it is not secret.
Explain requests for scheduling and limits for enforcement; CPU in millicores.
Derive the autoscaler formula and apply it.
Note autoscaling limits: min and max, stabilisation, node capacity.
examples: 4 replicas at 80 per cent CPU with a target of 50: ceil(4 x 80 / 50) = ceil(6.4) = 7.
A node with 4,000m allocatable CPU hosts 16 pods that each request 250m.

figures.shows: CPU per pod and replica count over time as load rises.
figures.learnerAction: Move the target and see replicas change.

figures.shows: A node bar of 4,000m filled with pod requests.
figures.learnerAction: Add pods until none more is schedulable.

questionPlan.sample: 4 replicas run at an average 80% CPU against a target of 50%. How many replicas does the autoscaler ask for?
A node has 4,000m allocatable CPU. Each pod requests 250m. How many pods fit by CPU?
What protects the contents of a Kubernetes Secret by default?
questionPlan.answer: Nothing beyond access control; it is only base64-encoded
choices: Nothing beyond access control; it is only base64-encoded

lessons.title: Infrastructure as code
lessons.objective: Read a declarative configuration, explain state, plan and drift, and predict what an apply will change.

concepts.title: Declarative description
concepts.summary: Files state what infrastructure should exist; the tool works out the steps.

concepts.title: State
concepts.summary: The tool's record of which real resources correspond to which declarations.

concepts.title: Drift
concepts.summary: A difference between the real infrastructure and its recorded or declared form, usually caused by manual change.

misconceptions: Running apply twice creates everything twice; a declarative tool compares and makes zero changes if nothing differs.
State is a cache you can delete; losing it makes the tool forget what it owns.
Console changes are fine if quick; they cause drift that the next apply may revert.
sequence: Contrast a shell script of commands with a declaration of the end result.
Walk the plan-then-apply cycle and read plan output.
Explain state, locking and why it is stored remotely and kept secret.
Show modules and variables as reuse, and environments as parameters.
Treat drift and review of plans in pull requests.
examples: count = 3 on a server resource declares 3 servers; raising it to 5 plans '2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy'.
Changing a server's instance type that forces replacement plans '1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy'.

figures.shows: Left: declared resources; middle: state; right: real resources, with differences highlighted.
figures.learnerAction: Make a manual change and see drift appear.

figures.shows: Plan output with symbols + - ~ and -/+.
figures.learnerAction: Match each symbol to its meaning.

questionPlan.sample: A configuration declares count = 3 servers and 3 already exist and match. Plan reports 'X to add, Y to change, Z to destroy'. Give X,Y,Z as three digits.
Count is raised from 3 to 5. How many resources does the plan add?
What is the term for real infrastructure differing from its declared form after a manual change?

lessons.title: GitOps, observability and reliability targets
lessons.objective: Explain a GitOps reconciler, distinguish metrics, logs and traces, and compute an error budget.

concepts.title: GitOps
concepts.summary: The desired state is stored in Git, and an agent in the cluster pulls and reconciles it continuously.

concepts.title: Metrics, logs and traces
concepts.summary: Numbers over time, discrete events, and the path of one request across services.

concepts.title: Error budget
concepts.summary: The allowed unreliability, equal to 1 minus the SLO, spent by outages and risky changes.

misconceptions: Pull-based deployment is slower; it removes cluster credentials from CI and corrects drift automatically.
Monitoring and observability are synonyms; monitoring checks known failures, observability supports asking new questions of the system.
A 100 per cent SLO is the safe target; it leaves no budget for change and costs disproportionately.
sequence: Show CI pushing to the cluster versus an agent pulling from Git.
Introduce the three signals and the question each answers.
Define SLI, SLO and the error budget.
Work the budget in minutes and a burn example.
Close with alerting on symptoms and on budget burn.
examples: 99.9 per cent over 30 days allows 30 x 24 x 60 x 0.001 = 43.2 minutes; 99.95 per cent allows 21.6; 99.99 per cent allows 4.32.
A 5.4-minute outage against a 21.6-minute budget spends 25 per cent.

figures.shows: Allowed downtime per 30 days against SLO from 99 to 99.99 per cent.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the SLO and read the minutes.

figures.shows: Request through three services with a trace waterfall, a latency graph and a log line.
figures.learnerAction: Click a signal to see what it reveals.

questionPlan.sample: An SLO of 99.9% over 30 days. How many minutes of downtime does the error budget allow?
The budget is 21.6 minutes and an outage lasts 5.4 minutes. What percentage of the budget is spent?
Which signal shows how one request travelled through several services?

lessons.title: Securing the pipeline and the supply chain
lessons.objective: Identify where a build can be attacked, and apply pinning, least-privilege credentials, scanning and signing.

concepts.title: Software supply chain
concepts.summary: Everything that enters a build: source, dependencies, base images, build tools and the pipeline itself.

concepts.title: Digest pinning
concepts.summary: Referring to an image by the SHA-256 of its content, so the reference cannot silently change.

concepts.title: SBOM
concepts.summary: A machine-readable list of the components in a built artifact.

misconceptions: Scanning images once is enough; new vulnerabilities are published against unchanged software.
A secret removed in a later commit is gone; it stays in history and must be rotated.
The CI system is trusted by default; it holds credentials and runs others' code, so it is a prime target.
sequence: Map the stages where an attacker can insert code: source, dependency, build, registry, deploy.
Pin by digest and lock files, with automated updates.
Keep secrets out of repositories and give pipelines short-lived, scoped credentials.
Scan dependencies and images, and produce an SBOM.
Sign artifacts and verify at deploy; mention SLSA levels as provenance maturity.
examples: A SHA-256 digest is 256 bits, written as 64 hexadecimal characters since each hex digit is 4 bits.
A tag such as node:22 can point to a different image next month; a digest cannot.

figures.shows: Pipeline stages with attack points numbered.
figures.learnerAction: Place a control on each attack point.

questionPlan.sample: A SHA-256 digest is written in hexadecimal. How many hexadecimal characters is it?
An access key was committed, then deleted in the next commit. What should be done?
What kind of list of components in an artifact is abbreviated SBOM?

courseCheck: Mixed check: DORA arithmetic, pipeline wall-clock time, canary traffic, layer-cache prediction, port mapping, rolling-update bounds, HPA replicas, plan output and error-budget minutes, plus choice questions on selectors, Secrets, drift and digests.
platformNeeds: A pipeline_stages figure type: stages with durations that can be dragged between serial and parallel lanes, with the total computed. Fallback: svg_figure with switchable views for fixed layouts.
A manifest_viewer figure: YAML or Dockerfile lines with a coloured annotation per line and a stepping cursor, for cache and rolling-update walkthroughs. Fallback: program_trace over the file's lines.
code-reading questions need a multi-line prompt that preserves Dockerfile and YAML layout (monospace block). No runner is needed.
A canary/rollout slider widget (traffic split with live error rate) would clearly help; fallback is data_series with a choice question.
unverified: No external site could be reached from the authoring session (network blocked), so every source has verified false: URLs and licences are from memory and must be checked.
Kubernetes rounding rule (maxSurge rounds up, maxUnavailable rounds down) and the HPA formula are recalled from the official docs and must be rechecked.
DORA 2024 rename of time to restore service to failed deployment recovery time, and 2014 as the first report year.
Docker, OpenGitOps, SLSA, OpenTofu and twelve-factor licences.
Version tag node:22 is only an example.
